title: What an unfed guest takes away
theme: The household continues: a guest left fasting in one’s house destroys the host’s hopes, merit, children and cattle.

words.context: Śaṅkara: āśā is longing for an unknown good, pratīkṣā waiting for a known one

words.meaning: pleasant and true speech (and its fruit)
the merit of sacrifices and of good works
words.context: Śaṅkara: iṣṭa the fruit of sacrifice, pūrta of works like gardens

sandhi.rule: A final n before c becomes anusvāra followed by ś, P. 8.3.7 (नश्छव्यप्रशान्) with P. 8.3.4 (अनुनासिकात्‌ परोऽनुस्वारः).
t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
a + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); the final n stands before v.

sandhi_exceptions.note: The base prints ca iṣṭāpūrte unjoined (Śaṅkara’s mūla); the vishvAsa mūla joins ceṣṭāpūrte (corrections.json).

samasa.meaning: the merit of sacrifices and of public works (the ā of iṣṭā- is the Vedic lengthening in this dvandva)

morphology.note: Present middle of vṛj (class 7, nasal infix), ‘wrench away, remove’. Raṅgarāmānuja notes the class-7 form and an alternative derivation.
Dual of a dvandva of two feminines. Śaṅkara distinguishes them: «अनिर्ज्ञातप्राप्येष्टार्थप्रार्थना आशा» and «निर्ज्ञातप्राप्यार्थप्रतीक्षणं प्रतीक्षा».

translation.literal: Hope and expectation, [the fruit of] company and pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and works, and sons and cattle, all — this he takes away from the man of little understanding in whose house a brāhmaṇa stays without eating.
translation.readable: ‘Hope and expectation, the good of friendship and kind words, the merit of rites and good works, sons and cattle — all of it is lost to the foolish man in whose house a brāhmaṇa stays unfed.’

anvaya: यस्य अल्पमेधसः पुरुषस्य गृहे ब्राह्मणः अनश्नन् वसति, [तस्य] आशाप्रतीक्षे सङ्गतम् सूनृताम् च इष्टापूर्ते सर्वान् पुत्रपशून् च एतत् [सः] वृङ्क्ते ॥
syntax: A long list of objects, summed up by etat (‘all this’), then the verb vṛṅkte and the genitive of the person deprived, with a relative clause (‘in whose house a brāhmaṇa stays unfed’). The subject of vṛṅkte is the unfed guest (or the fault of not feeding him).

ambiguities.topic: Who or what takes these away?
ambiguities.note: Grammatically the subject of vṛṅkte is the brāhmaṇa who stays unfed; Raṅgarāmānuja makes it the sin of his fasting, «एतत् अनशनरूपं पापं वृङ्क्ते».
Śaṅkara: the fruit of association with the good; Raṅgarāmānuja: the company of the good itself («सत्सङ्गमम्»).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Irregular triṣṭubh: 23 + 24 syllables as written. The first line counts the unjoined hiatus ca iṣṭāpūrte (22 if joined); the last pāda (yasyānaśnan vasati brāhmaṇo gṛhe) has twelve syllables, jagatī-like.

beginner: The household’s warning goes on. If a guest stays in your house without food, the consequences are drastic: everything you hope for and expect, the good that comes from friendship and kind words, the merit of your religious rites and charitable works, even your children and cattle — all of it is lost. The list is deliberately sweeping. It covers the future, social life, religious merit and family. The point is not a magical punishment so much as a judgement: a person who can leave a guest hungry has already lost what makes those good things good. And the warning is addressed to Death himself, who has let a boy wait three nights at his door.
analogy: Like a company that neglects a single customer so badly that word spreads and its whole reputation, built over years, collapses.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A brāhmaṇa who stays unfed in a foolish man’s house takes away his hopes and expectations, the fruit of company and kind speech, the merit of sacrifices and works, and his sons and cattle.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: āśā is «अनिर्ज्ञातप्राप्येष्टार्थप्रार्थना आशा», pratīkṣā «निर्ज्ञातप्राप्यार्थप्रतीक्षणं प्रतीक्षा»; iṣṭa and pūrta are «इष्टं यागजं फलं पूर्तम् आरामादिक्रियाजं फलम्». Raṅgarāmānuja: sūnṛtā is «सत्यप्रियवाचम्», speech both true and kind. Śaṅkara’s conclusion: «तस्मादनुपेक्षणीयः सर्वावस्थास्वप्यतिथिरित्यर्थः», a guest must never be neglected.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: A class-7 present of vṛj, ‘remove’: Śaṅkara glosses «वृङ्क्ते वर्जयति विनाशयतीत्येतत्». Raṅgarāmānuja gives the grammar (nasal infix, Dhātupāṭha references).

advaita.text: A warning that grounds the duty of hospitality: «तस्मादनुपेक्षणीयः सर्वावस्थास्वप्यतिथिरित्यर्थः».

visistadvaita.text: The household shows Yama the consequence of omission: the sin of the guest’s fasting destroys all — «एतत् अनशनरूपं पापं वृङ्क्ते».

schools.disagreement: No real disagreement; Madhva’s bhāṣya has no separate comment on this mantra.

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka uses the same pair, iṣṭāpūrta, for ritual merit — and warns against thinking it the highest. Here it is one of the goods a neglected guest destroys; later the Kaṭha too will look beyond it.

contemporary.text: Institutions that neglect the people who come to them in need may keep their assets for a while, but lose what those assets were for. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: Whose need in your life is easiest to overlook?
reflect.deeper: Why would neglecting one guest destroy merit gained in quite other ways?
reflect.practice: Offer food or drink to someone today who would not expect it from you.
